headline: High-risk pair: shared filesystem and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action hazards; compliance risk is moderate.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Kestra can read/write files and process workflow inputs, while oh-my-openagent uses runtime-injected MCPs/hooks and can read AGENTS.md/README.md. That creates a plausible shared-file or hook bridge where attacker-controlled content from one can influence the other. The pathway is documented by both profiles, though not directly observed.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or repo checkout
IF oh-my-openagent consumes AGENTS.md/README.md or hook output as instructions
IF Kestra writes workflow artifacts that the other agent later parses
mitigations: Disable automatic instruction parsing from shared files
Add provenance tags to files passed between agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: Kestra touches logs, inputs, database data, cloud storage data, messages, and notifications, and has broad network egress. oh-my-openagent touches project code, session history, and provider auth prompts, and also has broad egress. If they share a workspace or credentials, sensitive material can flow from one agent into the other's outputs or remote calls.
conditions: IF the two agents share files containing logs, database data, or auth prompts
IF either agent uploads its working context to external services
IF the same installation identity or credentials are reused across both
mitigations: Keep sensitive files out of shared directories
Rotate or scope credentials per agent
requires-engineering: add DLP controls on shared paths

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Kestra has execute_shell, read/write filesystem, subprocesses, and elevated root/docker.sock requests; oh-my-openagent has subprocesses, broad egress, browser access, and full-permissions mode. Both support multiple instances, so concurrent writes to shared files or mutable resources can race and corrupt state. The overlap is directly documented in both profiles.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same directory or git checkout
IF either agent uses shared mutable resources without locking
IF Kestra runs with root or docker.sock while oh-my-openagent runs full-permissions mode
mitigations: Serialize writes with a lock file
Run one agent at a time for mutable tasks
Restrict elevated privileges during shared operations

D_cascading_error.rationale: Kestra can generate workflow artifacts, logs, and notifications that oh-my-openagent may ingest through files, MCPs, or session history. Because oh-my-openagent has browser and messaging-oriented tooling, it can act on or relay those outputs without a built-in verification step shown here. That makes downstream mistakes or injected facts propagate into actions.
conditions: IF oh-my-openagent treats Kestra-produced artifacts as authoritative
IF either agent forwards unverified outputs into messages, tasks, or browser actions
IF workflow logs are used as source material for decisions
mitigations: Add a verification step between agents

E_compliance.rationale: Kestra touches database and cloud-storage data plus notifications, while oh-my-openagent handles provider auth prompts, session history, and project code. The profiles do not state residency or certification alignment, so a compliance mismatch is plausible but not proven. Uncertainty pushes this above low because both agents handle potentially regulated operational data.
conditions: IF regulated data such as customer records or auth prompts flows through both agents
IF the deployment spans jurisdictions with different residency rules
IF retention or deletion policies differ between the two systems
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared workflows
Restrict auth prompts to one agent
requires-engineering: align residency and compliance controls
